claims.claim: the kill-rate response is usually type II, rising to a plateau, in experiments with juvenile largemouth (Alexander et al. 2015; abstract only)
claims.source_value: juvenile largemouth bass showed a Type II functional response at every habitat complexity tested (zero to 2,700 artificial blades m⁻²), with no Type III; more complex habitat raised handling time and lowered maximum feeding rate
claims.location: manuscript p. 2 (PDF p. 3), Abstract, line 44; manuscript pp. 7–8 (PDF pp. 8–9), Results, lines 209–218
claims.quote: bass exhibited potentially population de-stabilising Type II functional responses
claims.conditions: laboratory, South Africa; 18 bass of 86.9 ± 2.5 mm TL (gape 14 mm) reused across treatments; female guppies 15–20 mm TL at 2–64 per 300-L tank; 4-h trials at 23 °C after 24 h without food; artificial vegetation at 0, 900, 1,800 and 2,700 blades m⁻²
claims.note: Full text now read: the '(abstracts only)' can be dropped for Alexander et al. Odd detail: the text reports attack rate falling as habitat became less complex while consumption rose (handling time fell more), so 'attack rate' here is not a simple search-efficiency measure.

notes: Consumption did not differ among zero, low and intermediate complexity and fell only at high complexity (2,700 blades m⁻²), suggesting a threshold. Prey survival without predators was > 98 %.
